q: Name the three domains of development and give an example of each.
a: Physical: body/brain changes, such as puberty. Cognitive: thinking changes, such as problem solving. Socioemotional: emotions/relationships, such as attachment.

q: How do nature, nurture, culture and society contribute to development?
a: Development reflects interaction between inherited characteristics and environmental experience, including culture and society. Neither alone is the whole explanation.

q: Put all eight Erikson crises in order.
a: Trust/mistrust; autonomy/shame and doubt; initiative/guilt; industry/inferiority; identity/role confusion; intimacy/isolation; generativity/stagnation; integrity/despair.

q: Match the first four Erikson crises to their guide age bands.
a: Birth-1: trust/mistrust. 1-3: autonomy/shame and doubt. 3-6: initiative/guilt. 6-12: industry/inferiority.

q: A teenager asks who she is and what she values. Which crisis is central?
a: Identity versus role confusion, in adolescence.

q: An adult mentors the next generation. Which Erikson crisis does this illustrate?
a: Generativity versus stagnation, in middle adulthood.

q: An older adult evaluates whether her life was meaningful. Which crisis is relevant?
a: Integrity versus despair, in late adulthood.

q: Contrast intimacy versus isolation with industry versus inferiority.
a: Intimacy: young adulthood, forming close relationships. Industry: school age, about 6-12 in the guide, developing competence.

q: Name Piaget's four stages in order and give the guide's age bands.
a: Sensorimotor 0-2; preoperational 2-7; concrete operational 7-11; formal operational about 12+.

q: A baby searches for a toy hidden under a cloth. What concept is shown?
a: Object permanence: understanding that the object continues to exist out of sight. It develops in the sensorimotor period.

q: A child says the taller glass contains more even though only the container changed. Which concept is missing?
a: Conservation. Preoperational thinking can focus on height; concrete operational thinking supports recognizing that quantity is unchanged.

q: A teenager reasons about a hypothetical law that does not exist. Which Piaget stage fits?
a: Formal operational, which supports abstract and hypothetical thinking.

q: Contrast assimilation and accommodation with an animal-category example.
a: Assimilation: calling a new four-legged animal a dog using an existing schema. Accommodation: revising the schema to distinguish dogs from cats.

q: Name Kohlberg's three moral levels and the basis of each.
a: Preconventional: personal consequences, punishment/reward. Conventional: rules/laws/social expectations. Postconventional: ethical principles, rights/justice.

q: Heinz should not steal because he will go to jail. Which moral level is this?
a: Preconventional. The reason centers on personal punishment, regardless of whether the decision is not to steal.

q: Heinz should not steal because laws must be obeyed. Which level is this?
a: Conventional. The justification centers on social rules and laws.

q: Heinz should steal because preserving life outweighs property rules. Which level can this represent?
a: Postconventional. The justification appeals to ethical principles rather than personal consequences or obedience alone.

q: What did Kohlberg evaluate in the Heinz dilemma: decision or reasoning?
a: The reasoning behind the decision. The same decision can be justified at different levels.

q: A baby crawls because of maturing muscles, brain, opportunities, motivation and practice. Which theory fits?
a: Dynamic systems theory: development emerges from multiple interacting factors.

q: Distinguish stable, continuous, stage, growth-and-decline, and unpredictable developmental patterns.
a: Stable stays relatively constant; continuous changes gradually; stage proceeds through distinct steps; growth-and-decline rises then falls; unpredictable does not follow one expected pattern.

q: Define teratogen and explain A D S.
a: A substance or environmental condition that can harm prenatal development. A D S: amount of exposure, duration, and developmental stage.

q: Why can the same teratogen affect development differently at different times?
a: Different organs and systems are developing at different stages. Timing, amount, and duration influence effects. There is no blanket guaranteed-safe first-two-week rule for smoking or alcohol.

q: How can experience, abuse or neglect affect the early brain?
a: Experience shapes neural connections. Abuse/neglect can disrupt attention, learning, emotional regulation, social development and brain development. Total size alone does not show healthy functioning.

q: Define rooting, sucking and grasping, and contrast early hearing and vision.
a: Rooting turns toward mouth-area touch; sucking supports feeding; grasping closes the hand. Hearing is relatively developed early; newborn vision is less mature and improves.

q: What did Harlow's surrogate-mother research show?
a: Contact comfort and security matter for attachment. Infant monkeys preferred a soft surrogate even when a wire surrogate provided food; attachment is not explained by food alone.

q: Compare secure, avoidant and resistant/ambivalent patterns in the Strange Situation.
a: Secure: caregiver is a base and reunion is comforting. Avoidant: little outward response/avoids contact. Resistant: distressed, seeks contact but resists comfort. Separation and reunion patterns matter.

q: A friend wrongly believes the keys are in the old location. You predict she will look there. What ability is shown?
a: Theory of mind: understanding that another person can hold thoughts or beliefs different from yours.

q: Explain adolescent risk-taking and classify all four parenting styles by warmth/control.
a: Reward/emotion systems can be active while planning/control systems develop. Authoritative high/high; authoritarian low/high; permissive high/low; uninvolved low/low. Exploration can support independence.

q: Name emerging adulthood's five characteristics and explain why peers are not always a negative influence.
a: Identity exploration, instability, self-focus, feeling in between, possibilities. Peers can encourage positive behavior and influence identity, choices and emotions.

q: Contrast normal older-age changes, dementia, fluid/crystallized intelligence and continued well-being.
a: Processing speed and some memory may decline; fluid intelligence concerns new problem solving, crystallized accumulated knowledge. Dementia is significant decline disrupting daily life, not inevitable aging. Activity, learning, relationships, purpose and healthy habits support function/well-being; the guide connects these with blue zones. Relationships and children can bring support, rewards and responsibilities.

q: What is learning? Distinguish the behaviorist and cognitive emphases in the notes.
a: A relatively permanent change in behavior or knowledge through experience. Behaviorist emphasis: changed behavior. Cognitive emphasis: changed mental representations of the environment.

q: Distinguish non-associative and associative learning.
a: Non-associative changes response to one stimulus. Associative learns a connection between events or between behavior and consequences.

q: You stop noticing traffic noise after repeated exposure. Which process is this?
a: Habituation: responding less strongly to a repeated stimulus.

q: After several loud bangs, you become more reactive to other noises. Which process is this?
a: Sensitization: stronger responding after exposure.

q: Define classical conditioning and name its associated researcher.
a: Learning associations between stimuli. A previously neutral stimulus acquires the ability to evoke a learned response. Ivan Pavlov.

q: Identify US and UR when food naturally produces salivation.
a: Food is the unconditioned stimulus; salivation to food is the unconditioned response.

q: A bell paired with food later elicits salivation. Identify CS and CR.
a: Bell is conditioned stimulus; salivation to the bell is conditioned response.

q: Why can salivation be either UR or CR?
a: The trigger differs. Salivation to food is unlearned; salivation to a learned food-predicting cue is conditioned.

q: What is acquisition?
a: The initial learning of an association between stimuli.

q: What happens when a bell is repeatedly presented without food and salivation declines?
a: Extinction of the conditioned response.

q: An extinguished response returns after a rest. What is this called?
a: Spontaneous recovery.

q: A response trained to one bell also occurs to a similar tone. Which process is this?
a: Stimulus generalization: similar stimuli elicit similar responses.

q: The dog responds to one food-predicting tone but not another. Which process is this?
a: Stimulus discrimination: learning to distinguish stimuli.

q: How does extinction differ from habituation?
a: Extinction reduces a learned conditioned response when the expected association is not maintained. Habituation reduces response to a repeated stimulus and need not involve a learned association.

q: Define operant conditioning and name its associated researcher.
a: Learning from consequences of behavior. B. F. Skinner.

q: What is Thorndike's law of effect?
a: Satisfying consequences make preceding behavior more likely to recur; unpleasant consequences make it less likely.

q: A rat presses a lever for food. What is the operant?
a: The lever-pressing behavior.

q: Explain the two dimensions in positive/negative reinforcement/punishment.
a: Positive adds something, negative removes something. Reinforcement increases behavior, punishment decreases it. Positive and negative do not mean good or bad.

q: Praise is added for studying, and studying increases. Classify it.
a: Positive reinforcement.

q: Buckling removes a warning beep, and buckling increases. Classify it.
a: Negative reinforcement.

q: An extra task is added after violations, and violations decrease. Classify it.
a: Positive punishment.

q: A desired privilege is removed, and rule-breaking decreases. Classify it.
a: Negative punishment.

q: How do continuous and partial reinforcement differ?
a: Continuous rewards every target response; partial/intermittent rewards only some responses.

q: A reward arrives after every ten sales. Which schedule is this?
a: Fixed ratio: a predictable number of responses.

q: A reward arrives after an unpredictable number of plays. Which schedule is this?
a: Variable ratio: an unpredictable number of responses.

q: The first eligible response after a set waiting period is rewarded. Which schedule is this?
a: Fixed interval: a predictable time interval before reinforcement becomes available.

q: The first eligible response after varying waiting periods is rewarded. Which schedule is this?
a: Variable interval: unpredictable time intervals before reinforcement becomes available.

q: Define shaping with a roll-over example.
a: Reinforcing successive approximations: reward lying down, then turning partly, then the full roll-over.

q: Define behavior modification and token economy.
a: Behavior modification applies learning principles to change target behaviors. A token economy gives tokens/points exchangeable for rewards. Tokens have learned, secondary reinforcing value.

q: What is preparedness, and why does biology matter?
a: A biological tendency to learn some associations more easily than others. Food-illness associations are a guide example; learning is not determined solely by rewards.

q: Explain latent learning and cognitive maps with a campus example.
a: Latent learning occurs without an immediate reward or visible performance change. A cognitive map is a mental layout: you learn campus by walking, then later use it to find a room.

q: What is insight learning?
a: Solving through a sudden realization of how the pieces fit together.

q: Define observational learning, modeling and vicarious conditioning.
a: Observational learning is learning by watching behavior/consequences. Modeling involves observation and imitation. Vicarious conditioning involves consequences experienced by someone else.

q: What did Bandura's Bobo doll work demonstrate?
a: Children can learn aggressive behavior by observing adults, without having to experience direct reinforcement for each action.

q: What are mirror neurons, and what is the final classical/operant/observational contrast?
a: Mirror neurons respond during some actions and observation of similar actions; studied in action understanding/imitation. Classical connects stimuli; operant connects behavior/consequences; observational learns by watching others. Mirror neurons are not a complete explanation of all observational learning.

q: Name the three phases of memory in order and define each.
a: Encoding gets information in; storage keeps it over time; retrieval accesses it. E S R.

q: How does selective attention affect encoding?
a: It focuses processing on some information while ignoring other input. Attention supports encoding but does not guarantee later recall.

q: Name and compare visual, acoustic and semantic coding.
a: Visual: appearance. Acoustic: sound. Semantic: meaning. Explaining a definition is semantic, not merely noticing how the word looks.

q: Contrast maintenance and elaborative rehearsal.
a: Maintenance repeats to keep information active. Elaborative connects meaning, examples and prior knowledge and generally supports longer-lasting learning better.

q: What is levels of processing? Give shallow and deep examples.
a: Depth of processing affects later memory. Shallow: noticing letters or sounds. Deep: explaining meaning and making connections.

q: Give four effective study actions and state the limitation about the Yanjaa video.
a: Attention, personal examples, explaining in your own words, retrieval practice, spaced review are accepted. The guide names the video but not its exact techniques; review the assigned video for those examples.

q: Remembering to buy milk later uses which memory type?
a: Prospective memory, remembering a future action.

q: Remembering last year's holiday uses which memory type?
a: Retrospective memory, recalling past events/information.

q: Contrast explicit and implicit memory.
a: Explicit involves conscious recollection that can usually be described. Implicit affects behavior/performance without requiring conscious recollection.

q: Classify knowing a definition versus recalling your first day of college.
a: Definition: semantic explicit memory. First day: episodic explicit memory.

q: What is procedural memory, and can it survive some explicit-memory impairments?
a: Memory for performing skills/actions, a form of implicit memory. Some skills can remain despite difficulty forming new explicit memories.

q: What is HSAM, and what does it not guarantee?
a: Highly superior autobiographical memory is unusual recall for personal life events, often dates. It is not perfect memory for all facts or learning.

q: What is flashbulb memory, and does confidence establish accuracy?
a: Vivid memory of the circumstances of learning surprising/emotional news. Confidence and vividness do not guarantee correct details.

q: Define coding, capacity and duration.
a: Coding: representational form. Capacity: amount held. Duration: time information remains available.

q: What is a schema, and how can it distort recall?
a: A framework organizing knowledge and expectations. It can help interpretation but also promote recalling expected details that were absent.

q: Explain association networks and neural network models.
a: Association networks represent connections between concepts. Neural network models use patterns of activation in interconnected units to represent information and explain learning/associations.

q: Match hippocampus, amygdala and prefrontal cortex to memory roles.
a: Hippocampus: new explicit memories/organizing experiences. Amygdala: emotional processing and emotional-memory influence. Prefrontal cortex: working memory, organization, strategic retrieval.

q: What roles do cortex, cerebellum and basal ganglia play?
a: Cortical areas represent/store different knowledge. Cerebellum and basal ganglia support aspects of motor learning, habits and other implicit memory.

q: What is long-term potentiation?
a: Lasting strengthening of communication between certain neurons after repeated/coordinated activity, one mechanism that may contribute to learning/memory.

q: Contrast consolidation and reconsolidation.
a: Consolidation stabilizes a new memory. Reconsolidation involves a retrieved memory becoming temporarily changeable and being stored again.

q: What is a retrieval cue? Give an example.
a: Information helping access memory, such as a song bringing back a holiday.

q: Contrast context-dependent and state-dependent memory.
a: Context-dependent involves similar external surroundings; state-dependent involves a similar internal state at learning and retrieval.

q: What is a mnemonic? Give two examples.
a: A memory aid for encoding/retrieval, such as an acronym, rhyme, image, memorable story or association. E S R is an example.

q: What pattern does Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve describe, and what study response follows?
a: Forgetting is often fastest soon after learning, then slows. Review across sessions instead of relying on one pass.

q: Contrast anterograde and retrograde amnesia.
a: Anterograde: trouble forming new long-term memories after onset. Retrograde: trouble recalling memories from before onset.

q: Your old password interferes with the new one. Which type of interference?
a: Proactive: older information interferes with new learning/recall.

q: Learning a new number makes the old one harder to recall. Which type?
a: Retroactive: newer information interferes with older recall.

q: Contrast blocking, absent-mindedness and persistence.
a: Blocking: temporary retrieval failure for stored information. Absent-mindedness: insufficient attention during learning/intended action. Persistence: unwanted recurring memories.

q: How does memory bias differ from source amnesia?
a: Bias: current feelings/beliefs influence past recollection. Source amnesia: information is remembered but its origin is forgotten.

q: What is cryptomnesia?
a: Mistaking a previously encountered idea for an original new idea.

q: What are suggestibility and false memories?
a: Suggestibility is susceptibility to misleading suggestions. A false memory is an event/detail recalled inaccurately or that did not happen as remembered.

q: What is the main lesson of Loftus's lost-in-a-shopping-mall study?
a: Suggestion can lead some participants to recollect an event that did not occur. It does not mean every memory is false; confidence/vividness alone are not proof.

q: Name the three storage systems of the Atkinson-Shiffrin model and their general sequence.
a: Sensory -> short-term -> long-term; attention and rehearsal/other processes matter, with retrieval later. The model is simplified, not a rigid one-way sequence.

q: How does the serial position effect relate to primacy and recency?
a: Beginning/end items are often better recalled. Primacy is beginning; recency is end.

q: Compare iconic and echoic memory and correct the notes' duration error.
a: Iconic is visual and generally lasts a fraction of a second. Echoic is auditory and can last several seconds. Four-to-five seconds is not the guide's iconic duration.

q: What did Sperling's partial-report method suggest?
a: Immediate cues allowed report of many letters from a selected part of an array, suggesting rich but very short-lived visual sensory storage exceeding full-report performance.

q: Give the guide's short-term-memory coding, capacity and unrehearsed duration.
a: Often acoustic, with visual/semantic coding also possible. Traditional capacity about 7±2 items; newer working-memory work often around 4 chunks in some tasks. Roughly 15-30 seconds without rehearsal; task conditions matter.

q: What is chunking, and does it make short-term storage unlimited?
a: Grouping separate pieces into meaningful units. It makes information easier to manage, not unlimited storage.

q: Contrast decay and interference.
a: Decay emphasizes weakening over time; interference emphasizes competition from other information.

q: Compare short-term and long-term memory.
a: Short-term: limited amount held briefly. Long-term: very large, relatively enduring storage of knowledge, experiences and skills for days/years/lifetime, though retrieval may fail and details may distort.
